payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
The argument for signed authorship assumes the author wants to be named. Across a working layer of the music business, the deal is the opposite. A ghost producer is paid, sometimes very well, on the explicit condition that the credit belongs to someone else, and the contract saying so is a standard instrument with decades of practice behind it, not an edge case a new system can wave away. The system that promises verifiable credit has, for this contributor, nothing to offer but exposure.

Paid to disappear

The arrangement reaches well past ghost production. Uncredited songwriting, work-for-hire session playing, demo vocals that survive into the final master, arrangement work folded into a producer's fee: each comes with paper assigning the public story to the buyer. The buyer is not a villain in this; anonymity is what was purchased, and both sides priced it. For these contracts, a provenance record that names every hand on a track is a breach notice with a verification link attached.

The easy fix is to leave those contributions out of the record, and it costs more than it appears to. A record with deliberate holes is a record whose completeness can never be asserted, and completeness is half of its value in a dispute. Worse, the hole sits exactly where disputes concentrate. The contributor with no public credit is the one most likely to come back years later claiming a share, which makes the gap where the ghost stood the most litigated square on the board.

The record is not the announcement

The conflict loosens once two acts stop being treated as one. Writing a record and publishing it are different events, and only the second one breaches anything. A contribution can be sealed at the moment of creation, bound to the specific work and the specific session, while nothing about it appears in public.

What the world sees is proof that a sealed claim exists and has not changed. Who it names stays inside the envelope, governed by the same contract that demanded the silence. The mathematics for this is old and plain: publish a fingerprint of the claim, keep the claim.

A · The sealed claim

Who it names

Kept inside the envelope, governed by the same contract that demanded the silence.

B · What the world sees

A fingerprint

Proof that a sealed claim exists and has not changed.

The seal has to be made at the session. A claim sealed after the fact proves only that someone eventually got around to making it, and the master itself holds no evidence to backfill the gap. The timing requirement is the same one the rest of the record lives under, and it is less obvious here because the ghost has every short-term incentive to skip it. Sealing feels unnecessary while the relationship is good, and the relationship is always good at the session.

The sealed claim matters when the contract fails

The sealed claim earns its keep the day the contract fails, and ghost deals fail in patterned ways. The flat fee that looked generous before the track became a catalog staple. A buyer who licenses the work into territory the agreement never covered.

In those moments a ghost with no sealed claim is arguing from old emails and memory, which is why so few of these disputes get past a lawyer's first read. A sealed claim from the session converts the argument from recollection into evidence, and the revelation becomes a choice made under the dispute's own rules rather than a condition of participating in the system at all.

What the mechanism cannot settle is custody. Somebody has to hold the sealed record through the years when nobody wants it opened, and every natural candidate for the job is a party to the interests it protects. The seal also cuts in both directions, since the buyer now holds dated proof of exactly what the ghost agreed to and for how much. Whether a court can compel the envelope open, and whether opening it breaches the very contract it was built to survive, are questions nobody has litigated yet.
payload.title: The credit that has to stay private
